Photograph: Ishtayaq Rasool Increasingly erratic weather patterns due to climate change mean people are losing homes, crops and livestock By Ishtayaq Rasool in Indian-administered Kashmir Wed 5 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A s rain lashed the Pir Panjal mountains before dawn on 19 July, Haji Mohammad Latief stepped outside his home in Murrah, a remote mountain village in Indian-administered Kashmir . His daughter had asked him to move the family’s car to a safer place as the rain got heavier. “I had only just parked it,” Latief recalled. “When I turned around, I saw the water coming.” Minutes later, a cloudburst sent mud, boulders and water crashing down the hillside. Latief, 48, had spent years building the house, where five generations of his Gujjar family lived together. Within minutes, the torrent swallowed it, trapping eight family members inside. He survived only because he had stepped outside. By dawn, everything he had built lay in rubble. When the Guardian reached Murrah four days later, electricity, roads and mobile networks were cut off. Floodwaters had washed away roads and footbridges, leaving the only way into the village a 90-minute walk through rain and landslide debris. Residents carried sacks of flour, cooking gas cylinders and medicines across the broken crossing. Murrah is perched high in the Pir Panjal range above the town of Bafliaz, in Poonch district, about 125 miles (200km) south-west of Srinagar, Kashmir’s main city. The village is home to mostly Gujjars, one of the largest pastoralist communities in the Himalayas, whose livelihoods have long depended on livestock, farming and seasonal migration through the mountains. The hillside remained too unstable for excavators to reach. Soldiers, disaster response teams and local volunteers searched the debris by hand while others combed the swollen Suran River for the missing. View image in fullscreen Rescue teams search for missing people in Murrah village after the cloudburst-triggered landslide. Photograph: Ishtayaq Rasool Latief now lives in the house of his brother, Mohd Bashir, just above the landslide. Inside, women gathered to mourn while men quietly received visitors offering condolences. Verses from the Qur’an echoed through the house. “I built that house for my family,” Latief said, holding up pictures of his 16-year-old son Sajjad Ahmed, an aspiring cricketer, whose body was still missing. Days before the disaster, the family recorded videos together. View image in fullscreen A photograph on a phone of 16-year-old Sajjad Ahmed, whose body remains missing Photograph: Ishtayaq Rasool As mourners gathered, news spread that another body had been found several miles down the river; the room fell silent as another funeral procession passed through the village. Among those searching was Mohammad Razak, 45, who had spent four days combing the river with a team of volunteers. “We’ve been searching every bend of the river,” he said. “We’re still hoping we’ll find them.” Murrah was among the worst-hit places after a series of cloudbursts, flash floods and landslides swept Jammu and Kashmir this month , killing at least 28 people. Scientists say rising temperatures are increasing the likelihood of short, intense rainfall events across the western Himalayas. In steep mountainous terrain, these rains can trigger rapid flooding and landslides, putting remote communities at increased risk. For mountain communities, the climate crisis is also exacerbating longstanding geographical and social vulnerabilities. View image in fullscreen Women gather on a rooftop as the funeral procession of the fourth recovered victim arrives in Murrah village Photograph: Ishtayaq Rasool The destruction stretched far beyond Murrah. About 30 miles away in Rajouri, the Manawar Tawi River burst its banks, washing away roads, dozens of vehicles and the town’s main Bela bus station. Low-lying settlements along the riverbank were submerged in mud and debris. Several houses collapsed across the Pir Panjal mountains, livestock were swept away and hundreds of families were displaced. About 180 miles north, in Gurez Valley near the line of control with Pakistan-administered Kashmir, residents say they are seeing the same pattern. A cloudburst in Achoora village on 20 July damaged the crops of 11 families and blocked the valley’s only road. Residents say increasingly erratic rainfall is disrupting farming and making traditional livelihoods more precarious. It followed a series of cloudbursts that hit Gurez and neighbouring Tulail over the past month, damaging homes, farmland, bridges, and roads. “People knew when the snow would come and when to plant crops,” said Aamir Asghar Khan, 26, a resident of Achoora. “Nothing seems predictable any more. The rain is getting more intense every year, and the frequent cloudbursts are threatening our livelihoods.” Heavy rainfall also triggered devastating floods and landslides in Ladakh and across the border in Pakistan-administered Gilgit-Baltistan, reinforcing concerns that increasingly erratic weather is affecting communities across the western Himalayas. The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development ( Icimod ) said the western Himalayas were experiencing frequent bursts of intense rainfall capable of triggering floods, landslides and cloudbursts. Accelerating glacier melt is likely to increase flood risks in the short term before reducing water availability in coming decades. “The challenge our mountain communities face is twofold – too much water at times and too little at others,” an expert from Icimod said. “Adaptation requires work on both fronts, managing flood risk and water scarcity together.” ICIMOD said priorities included expanding community-based early warning systems, installing more weather stations in high-altitude areas, restoring damaged watersheds and designing roads and other infrastructure for future weather conditions rather than historical weather patterns. View image in fullscreen Lower Murrah village in Poonch district. Photograph: Ishtayaq Rasool Dr Suheel Rasool Mir, a Kashmir-based sociologist who studies Indigenous communities in Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh, said pastoral communities were among the first to bear the consequences of erratic weather as their livelihoods relied directly on forests, rivers, grazing lands and seasonal migration. “For Gujjar, Bakarwal and Dard-Shin communities, these disasters are not simply natural hazards,” he said. “As climate extremes become more frequent, they lose not only homes and livestock but also the ecological knowledge and ancestral livelihoods that have sustained them for generations.” For Latief back in Murrah, only one hope remained. “I just want to find them,” he said. “Then we can bury our family together.” Explore more on these topics Kashmir India Natural disasters Climate crisis South and central Asia news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.dw.com/en/ebola-over-2-000-d.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Iec6 A health worker waits to be sprayed with disinfectant at a treatment center in Ituri, eastern Congo Image: Dieudonne Dirole/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) said on Tuesday that an outbreak of a particularly virulent strain of the Bundibugyo Ebola virus currently raging in the east and northeast of the country has killed more than 2,000 people since the first case was confirmed. In all, more than 4,380 infections have been recorded. The current outbreak is the 17th ever recorded in the DRC, with Sania Nishtar of the Gavi global vaccine alliance warning it could become "the largest outbreak ever." Until now, the worst outbreak recorded in the DRC was the one that took place from 2018 to 2020 when some 3,500 infections led to 2,300 deaths. The pace of death is gathering momentum this time around, with the virus spreading faster and exhibiting a higher mortality rate than the 2014-2016 West African outbreak — the worst outbreak on record, which logged 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths. Congo's Ebola outbreak exceeds 4,000 cases To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The current DRC outbreak was declared on May 15, but health authorities say the first transmissions likely took place in February of earlier still. The 1,000-death mark was not reached until nine weeks in, now — in just three-weeks' time — that figure has doubled again. The case fatality rate of the current outbreak is 45.9% compared to 39.6% in the 2014-2016 West African outbreak. 'We haven't reached the peak yet,' says DRC health minister Though there are vaccines against some strains of the Ebola virus, there are currently none approved for the rare Bundibugyo strain that is spreading across the DRC faster than health authorities can trace it. Moreover, health authorities face massive logistics challenges due to the volatile security situation in the country, where bad roads and rebel violence coupled with lack of healthcare worker pay and mass strikes make it increasingly difficult to keep tabs on the illness. "We haven't reached the peak yet," said Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba in an interview shared by the ministry on X. "Within the next three months, we expect to have already brought the spread under control and to start seeing it decline," he added. Ebola, which is transmitted through physical contact with bodily fluids, causing a hemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past half century. Authorities in the DRC have placed restrictions on public gatherings as well as closing the airport in Ituri Province, the epicenter of the outbreak. Still, fighting and disease have forced the displacement of masses of people in the DRC, Rwanda and South Sudan. On Monday, the World Health Organization's (WHO) regional director told reporters that authorities are "chasing the virus… the virus is ahead of us." WHO, DRC officials appeal to Congolese as Ebola spreads To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What's the latest on bids to treat or vaccinate this Ebola strain? Clinical trials for two antiviral treatment methods have been ongoing since early July and on Friday the WHO recommended undertaking a full-scale human trial of the Ervebo vaccine. Although Ervebo has proven effective against the Zaire strain of Ebola, its efficacy in fighting the Bundibugyo strain is unproven. WHO officials are hopeful that it can offer some protection against the DRC strain. Vaccine alliance Gavi says it has made some 500,000 doses of Ervebo in its stockpiles available for the trial. Virologists say the new Bundibugyo strain appears to have been transmitted from animals to humans and has changed from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012. Researchers from Congo, Uganda, Belgium and other countries published findings ‌in the journal Nature Medicine on Monday, suggesting the outbreak began ‌with an animal-to-human transmission event and was then spread between people. Given the severity of the outbreak, authorities are looking into the possibility that the pathogen may have mutated. Jean Kaseya, the head of the Africa CDC, last week warned that fewer and fewer new cases could be traced back to contacts of existing confirmed patients, with researchers falling well below the WHO's targets of tracking 95% of potential contacts to contain the spread.
